content.heading: 4.1 Vector Spaces and Subspaces
content.paragraph: Much of the theory in Chapters 1 and 2 rested on certain simple and obvious algebraic properties of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, listed in Section 1.3. In fact, many other mathematical systems have the same properties. The specific properties of interest are listed in the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A vector space is a nonempty set $V$ of objects, called vectors, on which are defined two operations, called addition and multiplication by scalars (real numbers), subject to the ten axioms (or rules) listed below.1 The axioms must hold for all vectors $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and $\mathbf{w}$ in $V$ and for all scalars $c$ and $d$.

list.item: The sum of u and v, denoted by u+v, is in V.
u+v=v+u.
There is a zero vector 0 in V such that u+0=u.
For each u in V, there is a vector −u in V such that u+(−u)=0.
The scalar multiple of u by c, denoted by cu, is in V.
c(u+v)=cu+cv.
(c+d)u=cu+du.
c(du)=(cd)u.
1u=u.

content.paragraph: Using only these axioms, one can show that the zero vector in Axiom $4$ is unique, and the vector $- \mathbf{u}$, called the negative of $\mathbf{u}$, in Axiom $5$ is unique for each $\mathbf{u}$ in $V$. See Exercises 33 and 34. Proofs of the following simple facts are also outlined in the exercises:

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: The spaces $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, where $n \geq 1$, are the premier examples of vector spaces. The geometric intuition developed for $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ will help you understand and visualize many concepts throughout the chapter.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $V$ be the set of all arrows (directed line segments) in three-dimensional space, with two arrows regarded as equal if they have the same length and point in the same direction. Define addition by the parallelogram rule (from Section 1.3), and for each $\textbf{v}$ in $V$, define $c\mathbf{v}$ to be the arrow whose length is $|c|$ times the length of $\textbf{v}$, pointing in the same direction as $\textbf{v}$ if $c \geq 0$ and otherwise pointing in the opposite direction. (See Figure 1.) Show that $V$ is a vector space. This space is a common model in physical problems for various forces.

image.alt: A figure shows three vectors with two vectors labeled v and 3 v pointing toward the upper right, and one vector labeled negative v pointing toward the lower left.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The definition of $V$ is geometric, using concepts of length and direction. No $xyz\text{-coordinate}$ system is involved. An arrow of zero length is a single point and represents the zero vector. The negative of $\textbf{v}$ is $( - 1)\mathbf{v}$. So Axioms $1$, $4$, $5$, $6$, and $10$ are evident. The rest are verified by geometry. For instance, see Figures 2 and 3.

image.alt: A figure shows four vectors joined together to form a parallelogram.
A figure shows four vectors joined together to form a trapezoid.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $\mathbb{S}$ be the space of all doubly infinite sequences of numbers (usually written in a row rather than a column):

If $\{ z_{k}\}$ is another element of $\mathbb{S}$, then the sum $\{ y_{k}\} + \{ z_{k}\}$ is the sequence $\{ y_{k} + z_{k}\}$ formed by adding corresponding terms of $\{ y_{k}\}$ and $\{ z_{k}\}$. The scalar multiple $c\,\{ y_{k}\}$ is the sequence $\{ cy_{k}\}$. The vector space axioms are verified in the same way as for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.

Elements of $\mathbb{S}$ arise in engineering, for example, whenever a signal is measured (or sampled) at discrete times. A signal might be electrical, mechanical, optical, biological, audio, and so on. The digital signal processors mentioned in the chapter introduction use discrete (or digital) signals. For convenience, we will call $\mathbb{S}$ the space of (discrete-time) signals. A signal may be visualized by a graph as in Figure 4.

image.alt: A graph titled Figure 4: A discrete-time signal depicts the shape of a discrete-time signal.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: For $n \geq 0$, the set $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ of polynomials of degree at most $n$ consists of all polynomials of the form

where the coefficients $a_{0}\text{,\,\,…\,\,,\,}a_{n}$ and the variable $t$ are real numbers. The degree of $\mathbf{p}$ is the highest power of $t$ in (4) whose coefficient is not zero. If $\mathbf{p}(t) = a_{0} \neq 0$, the degree of $\mathbf{p}$ is zero. If all the coefficients are zero, $\mathbf{p}$ is called the zero polynomial. The zero polynomial is included in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ even though its degree, for technical reasons, is not defined.
If $\mathbf{p}$ is given by (4) and if $\mathbf{q}(t) = b_{0} + b_{1}t + \cdots + b_{n}t^{n}$, then the sum $\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}$ is defined by
The scalar multiple $c\mathbf{p}$ is the polynomial defined by

These definitions satisfy Axioms $1$ and $6$ because $\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}$ and $c\mathbf{p}$ are polynomials of degree less than or equal to $n$. Axioms $2$, $3$, and $7–10$ follow from properties of the real numbers. Clearly, the zero polynomial acts as the zero vector in Axiom $4$. Finally, $( - 1)\mathbf{p}$ acts as the negative of $\mathbf{p}$, so Axiom $5$ is satisfied. Thus $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ is a vector space.
The vector spaces $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ for various $n$ are used, for instance, in statistical trend analysis of data, discussed in Section 6.8.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $V$ be the set of all real-valued functions defined on a set $\mathbb{D}$. (Typically, $\mathbb{D}$ is the set of real numbers or some interval on the real line.) Functions are added in the usual way: $\mathbf{f} + \mathbf{g}$ is the function whose value at $t$ in the domain $\mathbb{D}$ is $\mathbf{f}(t) + \mathbf{g}(t)$. Likewise, for a scalar $c$ and an $\mathbf{f}$ in $V$, the scalar multiple $c\mathbf{f}$ is the function whose value at $t$ is $c\mathbf{f}(t)$. For instance, if $\mathbb{D} = {\mathbb{R}}$, $\mathbf{f}(t) = 1 + \sin 2t$, and $\mathbf{g}(t) = 2 + .5t$, then

Two functions in $V$ are equal if and only if their values are equal for every $t$ in $\mathbb{D}$. Hence the zero vector in $V$ is the function that is identically zero, $\mathbf{f}(t) = 0$ for all $t$, and the negative of $\mathbf{f}$ is $( - 1)\mathbf{f}$. Axioms $1$ and $6$ are obviously true, and the other axioms follow from properties of the real numbers, so $V$ is a vector space.

content.paragraph: It is important to think of each function in the vector space $V$ of Example 5 as a single object, as just one “point” or vector in the vector space. The sum of two vectors $\mathbf{f}$ and $\mathbf{g}$ (functions in $V$, or elements of any vector space) can be visualized as in Figure 5, because this can help you carry over to a general vector space the geometric intuition you have developed while working with the vector space $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. See the Study Guide for help as you learn to adopt this more general point of view.

content.heading: Subspaces
content.paragraph: In many problems, a vector space consists of an appropriate subset of vectors from some larger vector space. In this case, only three of the ten vector space axioms need to be checked; the rest are automatically satisfied.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A subspace of a vector space $V$ is a subset $H$ of $V$ that has three properties:

list.item: The zero vector of V is in H.2
H is closed under vector addition. That is, for each u and v in H, the sum u+v is in H.
H is closed under multiplication by scalars. That is, for each u in H and each scalar c, the vector cu is in H.

content.paragraph: Properties (a), (b), and (c) guarantee that a subspace $H$ of $V$ is itself a vector space, under the vector space operations already defined in $V$. To verify this, note that properties (a), (b), and (c) are Axioms $1$, $4$, and $6$. Axioms $2$, $3$, and $\text{7–10}$ are automatically true in $H$ because they apply to all elements of $V$, including those in $H$. Axiom $5$ is also true in $H$, because if $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H$, then $( - 1)\textbf{u}$ is in $H$ by property (c), and we know from equation (3) earlier in this section that $( - 1)\textbf{u}$ is the vector $- \textbf{u}$ in Axiom $5$.

So every subspace is a vector space. Conversely, every vector space is a subspace (of itself and possibly of other larger spaces). The term subspace is used when at least two vector spaces are in mind, with one inside the other, and the phrase subspace of $V$ identifies $V$ as the larger space. (See Figure 6.)

image.alt: A figure shows a shaded parallelogram labeled V, representing the vector space. A diagonal line passes through the center 0 without touching the corners. The area above the diagonal line is labeled H.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: The set consisting of only the zero vector in a vector space $V$ is a subspace of $V$, called the zero subspace and written as $\{ 0\}$.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Let $\text{ℙ}$ be the set of all polynomials with real coefficients, with operations in $\text{ℙ}$ defined as for functions. Then $\text{ℙ}$ is a subspace of the space of all real-valued functions defined on $\text{ℝ}$. Also, for each $n \geq 0$, $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ is a subspace of $\text{ℙ}$, because $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ is a subset of $\text{ℙ}$ that contains the zero polynomial, the sum of two polynomials in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ is also in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$, and a scalar multiple of a polynomial in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ is also in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: The set of finitely supported signals $\mathbb{S}_{f}$ consists of the signals $\{ y_{k}\}$, where only finitely many of the $y_{k}$ are nonzero. Since the zero signal $0 = \left( \text{…}\text{,~}0\text{,~}0\text{,~}0\text{,~…} \right)$ has no nonzero entries, it is clearly an element of $\mathbb{S}_{f}$. If two signals with finitely many nonzeros are added, the resulting signal will have finitely many nonzeros. Similarly if a signal with finitely many nonzeros is scaled, the result will still have finitely many nonzeros. Thus $\mathbb{S}_{f}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{S}$, the discrete-time signals. See Figure 7.

image.alt: Two graphs show the signals c plus d, c, and d on the left and signals b c, and c on the right.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: The vector space $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ is not a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ because $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ is not even a subset of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. (The vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ all have three entries, whereas the vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ have only two.) The set
is a subset of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ that “looks” and “acts” like $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, although it is logically distinct from $\text{ℝ}^{2}$. See Figure 8. Show that $H$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$.

figure.label: Figure 8
figure.caption: The x1x2-plane as a subspace of ℝ3

image.alt: A figure shows a rectangular plane representing the sub-space resting on a three-dimensional axis facing perpendicular to the third axis.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The zero vector is in $H$, and $H$ is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication because these operations on vectors in $H$ always produce vectors whose third entries are zero (and so belong to $H$). Thus $H$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$.

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: A plane in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ not through the origin is not a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, because the plane does not contain the zero vector of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. Similarly, a line in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ not through the origin, such as in Figure 9, is not a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{2}$.

figure.label: Figure 9
figure.caption: A line that is not a vector space

image.alt: A graph shows a straight line on a coordinate plane.

content.heading: A Subspace Spanned by a Set
content.paragraph: The next example illustrates one of the most common ways of describing a subspace. As in Chapter 1, the term linear combination refers to any sum of scalar multiples of vectors, and $\text{Span~}\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\mathbf{v}_{p}\}$ denotes the set of all vectors that can be written as linear combinations of $\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\mathbf{v}_{p}.$

example.heading: Example 11
example.paragraph: Given $\mathbf{v}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{2}$ in a vector space $V$, let $H = \text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\}$. Show that $H$ is a subspace of $V$.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The zero vector is in $H$, since $0 = 0\mathbf{v}_{1} + 0\mathbf{v}_{2}$. To show that $H$ is closed under vector addition, take two arbitrary vectors in $H$, say,
By Axioms $2$, $3$, and $8$ for the vector space $V$,
So $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ is in $H$. Furthermore, if $c$ is any scalar, then by Axioms $7$ and $9$,
which shows that $c\mathbf{u}$ is in $H$ and $H$ is closed under scalar multiplication. Thus $H$ is a subspace of $V$.

content.paragraph: In Section 4.5, you will see that every nonzero subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, other than $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ itself, is either $\text{Span}~\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$ for some linearly independent $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$ or $\text{Span~}\{\textbf{v}\}$ for $\textbf{v} \neq 0$. In the first case, the subspace is a plane through the origin; in the second case, it is a line through the origin. (See Figure 10.) It is helpful to keep these geometric pictures in mind, even for an abstract vector space.

image.alt: A figure shows a rectangular plane resting on a three-dimensional coordinate facing perpendicular to the third axis.

content.paragraph: The argument in Example11 can easily be generalized to prove the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem 1
note.heading: Theorem 1
note.paragraph: If $\textbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\textbf{v}_{p}$ are in a vector space $V$, then $\text{Span\,\,\,\{}\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{p}\text{\}}$ is a subspace of $V$.

content.paragraph: We call $\text{Span~}\{\textbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\textbf{v}_{p}\}$ the subspace spanned by (or generated) $\{\textbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\textbf{v}_{p}\}$. Given any subspace $H$ of $V$, a spanning set (or generating) for $H$ is a set $\{\textbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\textbf{v}_{p}\}$ in $H$ such that $H = \text{Span}\{\textbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\text{…}\text{,}\textbf{v}_{p}\}$.
The next example shows how to use Theorem 1.

example.heading: Example 12
example.paragraph: Let $H$ be the set of all vectors of the form $(a - 3b\text{,~}b - a\text{,~}a\text{,~}b)$, where $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary scalars. That is, let $H = \{(a - 3b\text{,~}b - a\text{,~}a\text{,~}b):a$ and $b$ in $\text{ℝ}\text{\}}$. Show that $H$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{4}$.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Write the vectors in $H$ as column vectors. Then an arbitrary vector in $H$ has the form

This calculation shows that $H = \text{Span~}\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$, where $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$ are the vectors indicated above. Thus $H$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{4}$ by Theorem 1.

content.paragraph: Example 12 illustrates a useful technique of expressing a subspace $H$ as the set of linear combinations of some small collection of vectors. If $H = \text{Span~}\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\textbf{v}_{p} \right\}$, we can think of the vectors $\textbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\textbf{v}_{p}$ in the spanning set as “handles” that allow us to hold on to the subspace $H$. Calculations with the infinitely many vectors in $H$ are often reduced to operations with the finite number of vectors in the spanning set.

example.heading: Example 13
example.paragraph: For what value(s) of $h$ will $\mathbf{y}$ be in the subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ spanned by $\textbf{v}_{1}$, $\textbf{v}_{2}$, $\textbf{v}_{3}$, if
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: This question is Practice Problem 2 in Section 1.3, written here with the term subspace rather than ${Span}\,\left\{ {\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}} \right\}$. The solution there shows that $\mathbf{y}$ is in ${Span}\,\left\{ {\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}} \right\}$ if and only if $h = 5$. That solution is worth reviewing now, along with Exercises 11–16 and 19–21 in Section 1.3.

content.paragraph: Although many vector spaces in this chapter will be subspaces of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, it is important to keep in mind that the abstract theory applies to other vector spaces as well. Vector spaces of functions arise in many applications, and they will receive more attention later.
